name: Economists and Labor
blurb: Economists and labour researchers measuring what AI does to work, wages and productivity.

reading.body:
Erik Brynjolfsson's three decades of measuring how digital technology affects productivity and employment have moved from academic research into corporate strategy, as generative AI forced every company to confront questions he had already quantified.

The economists and labor researchers tracked here study AI's actual impact on work, wages, and productivity rather than speculating about it. Brynjolfsson's shift from publishing in academic journals to advising boardrooms reflects a broader shift: AI's effects on labor are no longer theoretical. Companies now need empirical answers to the questions Brynjolfsson had been answering for years. This matters because scaling AI at the pace required by compute and power constraints will reshape employment faster than policy, retraining, or social safety nets can easily absorb.

The data does not cover wage distribution, regional impact, or the timeline of job displacement versus job creation. It does not measure whether retraining programs like those Steve Preston directs at Goodwill can match the pace of AI-driven automation. It shows only that the people measuring AI's labor effects now operate across three worlds: academic research, political advocacy, and nonprofit implementation. That convergence itself is a signal that the question has moved from whether AI displaces labor to how quickly and who bears the cost.

profiles.hook: Brynjolfsson has spent three decades building the empirical case for how digital technology, and now AI, actually changes productivity and jobs, work that shifted from academic papers to boardroom strategy as generative AI forced every company to ask the same question he had been measuring for years.
profiles.name: Erik Brynjolfsson
profiles.moniker: Economist of the Second Machine Age
